title: Abba Moses and the leaking basket
hookLine: asked to judge a brother, he arrives carrying a basket leaking sand: my own faults run out behind me (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)

lines: DID YOU HEAR WHAT HE DID?
cards: Someone messes up, and the group chat lights up. Did you hear what he did? Can you believe she said that?

It's a strange kind of fun, deciding together how wrong someone else was. Now move the scene to the Egyptian desert. A community of early Christian monks has gathered to sit in judgment on one of their brothers.
They're waiting for one more elder, a big, well-known old man named Moses. And when he finally walks in, he's carrying something odd.

teach.b: Early Christian monks went out into the deserts of Egypt to live simply and pray.
They called their elders abba, father, and the elders' short, sharp sayings were later written down as the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, still read in monasteries today.

Abba Moses is a surprise among them. Tradition says he came from Ethiopia, was once a servant and then the leader of a gang of robbers, before he turned up at a monastery and slowly became one of its gentlest elders.
At the settlement of Scetis, a brother does something wrong. The monks call a council and send for Moses. He doesn't want to come.
They send again: everyone is waiting for you.

So he goes, carrying a container full of holes, with something running out behind him the whole way. In the Greek sayings, it's a jug, leaking water; later retellings make it a basket, trickling sand.
The monks come out to meet him and ask: father, what is this?

teach.h: MY FAULTS RUN OUT BEHIND ME.
teach.b: And Moses says, more or less: my own faults are running out behind me, and I don't even see them, and today I've come to judge somebody else's. That's all.
The story says the monks said nothing more to the brother, and forgave him.
He doesn't say the brother did nothing wrong. He doesn't give a speech about mercy. He walks in carrying the truth about himself where everyone can see it, and the room changes.
The trail behind him is the whole sermon.

how: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers are read in Orthodox, Coptic, Catholic and some Protestant communities, and Abba Moses is honored as a saint; the leaking basket is often told when people talk about not judging.

a basket of sand carried as a penance
a council of monks that judges a brother

p: father: the title for a desert elder
the leader of a gang of robbers

games.q: you're Abba Moses. the monks have gathered to judge a brother and they're waiting for you. what do you do?
o: walk in and give the harshest verdict
refuse and stay in your cell
games.why: he refuses at first, then comes carrying a leaking container: my own faults run out behind me, and I've come to judge another's. the monks forgive the brother.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've been quietly judging, a coworker, a relative, a stranger online, and just notice the judgment without arguing with it.
Now picture walking toward them carrying Moses's basket, a thin line of sand running out behind you: a few of your own old mistakes, the ones you'd rather nobody mentioned.
You don't have to drop the judgment; carry the basket alongside it, and feel what happens.

wordCard.voice: Scetis. The desert settlement where an elder came to a trial carrying his own faults behind him, in a basket that leaked the whole way.

orig.note: Aramaic: father. the desert monks used abba as the title for a respected elder.

carryVoice: Your line: my own basket leaks. The judge carries faults too, whether he sees them or not. That's day seventy-three.
